questions.prompt: Isaiah 11 lists seven gifts of the Holy Spirit that rest upon the Messiah and, through him, upon believers. Which of these is one of the seven?
choices: Wisdom
Patience
Kindness
Self-control
questions.explanation: The seven gifts are wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. Patience, kindness, and self-control are instead traditionally counted among the fruits of the Spirit, not the gifts.
questions.hint: The other three options are actually fruits of the Spirit, not gifts -- a different, though related, list.

citations.quote: The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: a spirit of wisdom and of understanding, a spirit of counsel and of strength, a spirit of knowledge and of fear of the Lord.

questions.prompt: True or False: The 'fruits of the Spirit,' as listed by St. Paul in Galatians, include love, joy, peace, and patience.
questions.explanation: Paul's list in Galatians 5:22-23 begins: 'love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control' -- visible signs that the Spirit is truly at work in a life.
questions.hint: This list comes from Paul's letter to the Galatians, right after his list of the 'works of the flesh.'

citations.quote: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

questions.prompt: The Catechism describes the fruits of the Spirit as the first ____ of eternal glory -- perfections formed in us as the Spirit's work begins to bear visible results.
questions.explanation: The image is agricultural: just as a tree's fruit shows the tree is healthy, the Spirit's fruits in a soul are the first, visible signs of the glory that awaits in full at the end.
questions.hint: It's the same word already used earlier in the sentence, describing what these perfections are called.

citations.quote: The fruits of the Spirit are perfections that the Holy Spirit forms in us as the first fruits of eternal glory.

questions.prompt: The seven gifts of the Holy Spirit (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord) exist to:
choices: Complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them
Replace the need for faith, hope, and charity entirely
Benefit only priests and consecrated religious
Apply only to the twelve apostles historically
questions.correctAnswer: Complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them
questions.explanation: The gifts don't compete with the virtues -- they make a person docile to the Holy Spirit's promptings, perfecting the virtues so a person can respond readily to God's inspiration.
questions.hint: Think of these gifts as fine-tuning the virtues already present, not replacing them.

citations.quote: The gifts of the Holy Spirit... complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them. They make the faithful docile in readily obeying divine inspirations.

questions.prompt: True or False: 'Fear of the Lord,' as one of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, means being terrified of God as a harsh, arbitrary judge.
questions.explanation: This gift means filial reverence and awe before God's holiness and goodness -- the fitting response of a child toward a father worthy of total respect -- not the servile terror of someone facing an unpredictable tyrant.
questions.hint: Think of a child's reverent respect for a good father, not dread of a threatening stranger.

citations.quote: The gifts of the Holy Spirit... complete and perfect the virtues of those who receive them.

questions.prompt: Match each list to where it comes from and how it's acquired.

pairs.left: Seven gifts of the Holy Spirit

pairs.right: Developed through human effort and habit

questions.explanation: These four lists work together in the spiritual life: virtues form good habits, gifts make us docile to the Spirit, and fruits are the visible evidence the Spirit is truly at work.
questions.hint: Two of these pairs point to a Scripture source; two point to how the virtues are acquired.

citations.quote: The spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: a spirit of wisdom and of understanding, a spirit of counsel and of strength, a spirit of knowledge and of fear of the Lord.
The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, generosity, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.

questions.prompt: How do the gifts of the Holy Spirit differ from the theological virtues in their manner of operating?
choices: The gifts make a person docile to the Spirit's own promptings, acting almost by instinct rather than by reasoned deliberation each time
The gifts are acquired through practice, unlike the virtues
The gifts operate only in the ordained
There is no real difference between them
questions.correctAnswer: The gifts make a person docile to the Spirit's own promptings, acting almost by instinct rather than by reasoned deliberation each time
questions.explanation: A virtue disposes a person to act well through their own deliberation; a gift disposes them to be readily moved by the Spirit, sometimes faster than reasoning could work through the situation. This is why the saints are often described as acting rightly 'instinctively.'
questions.hint: Ask who is doing the prompting in each case — the person's own reasoning, or something received.

questions.prompt: True or False: The fruits of the Spirit are the same thing as the gifts of the Spirit, just listed with different words.
questions.explanation: False. The gifts are the seven dispositions that make a person receptive to the Spirit's movement; the fruits (Galatians lists love, joy, peace, and others) are what results when the gifts are actually lived out — the perfections the Catechism calls 'first fruits of eternal glory.' One is the receiving capacity, the other the visible harvest.
questions.hint: Ask which comes first, a capacity to receive or a result that is produced.

questions.prompt: 'Fear of the Lord' among the seven gifts does not mean terror, but ____ — a profound reverence for God's majesty and dread of offending the One we love.
questions.explanation: This is filial fear, the fear of a child who dreads disappointing a father he loves, not servile fear of punishment from a stranger. The distinction matters pastorally: someone taught only servile fear of God has been taught something less than what the gift actually names.
questions.hint: Compare the fear a child has of disappointing a parent to the fear of a stranger with power over you.

questions.prompt: Match each list to where it comes from and how it operates.

pairs.right: Acquired by human effort and habituation
Infused by God, directed to God himself
Received dispositions making a person docile to the Spirit
The visible result when the gifts are lived, first fruits of glory

questions.explanation: These four lists are often blurred together in casual speech. Keeping them distinct is what lets someone locate a real spiritual difficulty precisely — a failure of habituation is not the same problem as a failure to be docile to grace.
questions.hint: Read down the list as a sequence: built by us, given to us, received as capacity, and shown as result.
